context_chunks.text: Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout.

Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["

", "


"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust.

**Customer content (MUST remain within pinned region(s))**
- Prompt / messages / input text (including system prompts provided by customer)
- Tool/function call arguments provided by customer
- Uploaded documents or retrieved passages (RAG payloads) provided by customer
- Model outputs (including partial streaming tokens)
- Embeddings input text and embeddings vectors derived from customer text
- Rerank inputs (candidate passages) and rerank outputs derived from those passages
- Fine-tuning / adapter payloads if routed through Hosted API pathways (not in scope for v1 feature, but classification applies)
- Any debug payloads that include raw request/response bodies
- Any derived artifacts that can reconstruct content (e.g., token logs, decoded segments, sampled prompt fragments)

**Not customer content (may be processed outside pinned region(s) under constraints below)**
- Non-content operational metadata that does not include request/response bodies and cannot reasonably be used to reconstruct them (see “Allowed cross-region metadata”). Notes:
- Whether content includes PII is not determinative; **all prompts/outputs are treated as sensitive content**. - “Derived” includes transformations (tokenization, embedding vectors, compression) if they are computed from customer text/output. ### 2) Enforcement boundary: “Where residency applies”
For pinned orgs/projects/API keys, **all handling of customer content** must remain in allowed region(s) for:
- **Request routing** and execution (including retries and fallbacks)
- **Background work** that uses the request payload or output (e.g., async logging of bodies, eval capture, replay queues)
- **Persistence and caching** of any form of request/response content
- **Observability signals** that contain content (logs/traces/debug captures)

Residency enforcement is evaluated at request time by the gateway/routing policy engine and must be **deterministic** (same policy + same request context → same allow/block outcome).

Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI Responses family expect stable streaming semantics, reliable tool/function call signal delivery, and preservation of determinism hints (seed/RNG) and user metadata when we bridge from our internal Responses v9-compatible runtime to the OpenAI API shape. This PR adds a resilience layer that: 1) performs backpressure-aware chunking and reassembly for streaming frames to avoid partial json/toolcall corruption on slow clients, 2) proxies a lightweight 'tool-signal' envelope so function/tool-calling boundaries are deterministic across retries and reconnections, and 3) forwards seed/determinism flags and a subset of user metadata transparently through the compatibility layer. What this changes (summary): consistent chunk framing and reassembly on the server and client-facing bridge; explicit tool-signal envelope that annotates tool-call start/end + unique tool invocation id; passthrough of 'rng_seed' and 'deterministic' attributes from our Responses request model into the OpenAI-compatible response attributes; metadata routing (user-provided tags/trace id) added to response attributes and to audit logs so downstream services (console, evals) see the same identifiers. Compatibility notes: We keep the OpenAI-compatible surface stable for existing callers. Default behavior is identical unless callers set determinism/seed or rely on streaming reconnects; in those cases the bridge guarantees idempotent framing (replay-safe chunk markers) and consistent toolcall reassembly. There are small opt-ins: the 'tool-signal' envelope is only applied when callers include a 'enable_tool_signal' flag (default true for our hosted API). For private deployments customers can opt-out via config.

Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. Checklist: [x] unit tests for stream finalizer [x] integration test that simulates disconnect + resume [x] docs page and compatibility notes [x] change log entry. Summary:

On 2026-04-25 at ~02:12 UTC the hosted streaming API experienced a high-severity outage that manifested as 5xx errors for streaming sessions and extreme tail latency for non-streaming requests. Impact lasted ~43 minutes for customers on affected regions and degraded for another 90 minutes during mitigation rollouts. Root cause: an unintended change to a per-connection TTL/keepalive config combined with an edge buffer write-stall bug in the streaming proxy, which caused head-of-line stalls and backlog amplification under normal traffic spikes.

Impact:
- Scope: ~11% of streaming sessions experienced repeated 5xx (502/504) immediately; additional ~7% of non-streaming requests saw 95th+ latency spikes from 600ms -> 3.2s.
- Customers: 23 enterprise tenants saw visible error rates; a handful of PLG customers reported degraded developer experience. No data loss or model correctness issues were observed.
- Business: Incidents triggered PagerDuty P0 and on-call SREs initiated incident response. External status page was updated.

How it was detected:
- First alert: custom anomaly detector on streaming session error-rate crossed threshold at 02:13 UTC (SRE paging).
- Secondary signals: edge response-time dashboards and increased connection resets observed in edge logs.
- Pager: 02:14 UTC, SRE lead ack at 02:15 UTC.

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:12 — initial spike in streaming session errors; error rate rose from baseline 0.3% to 18% in 2 minutes.
- 02:13 — anomaly alert fires; on-call SRE starts investigation.
- 02:14 — correlating logs show write stall metrics on streaming proxy (high write queue depth).
- 02:18 — quick mitigation: rolling restart of streaming-proxy fleet in affected region, partial drop in errors but tail latency persisted.
- 02:25 — rollback of a recent edge-config change that adjusted connection TTL made at 01:55 UTC.

- 02:35 — error rates fall to ~2%; tail latency trending down but not fully recovered.
- 02:55 — full rollback complete and additional throttling rules temporarily applied; streaming success rates returned to baseline.
- 03:00 — status page updated to reflect mitigation progress.
- 04:30 — follow-up remediation runs and validation; monitoring shows stable behavior. Incident declared mitigated at 04:35.

Root cause analysis (why):
- Primary bug: an existing bug in streaming-proxy write handling where a stalled TCP write (EAGAIN/later drain) could leave per-connection buffers frozen while the proxy's internal queue accounting incorrectly marked the connection as writable. This allowed the proxy to continue accepting streaming state and buffer memory without advancing network writes, producing head-of-line stalls.
- Trigger: a separately deployed edge config tweak at 01:55 UTC reduced keepalive/TTL for upstream connections from 90s -> 10s to aggressively free idle connectors for recent scaling changes.

- Plugin correctness SLO for promoted validators: >= 99.5% successful runs on representative slices during a 72-hour shadow window. - Performance SLO: median per-probe latency should be within 3x of the canonical evaluator for the same slice at promotion time. - Safety gate: any run producing >0.5% hallucination-class failures on audited probes must block auto-promotion.

Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

According to the proposed canonical order for v1 (ADR-042), the priority order for evaluating failure signals is as follows:

1.  **Reachability DOWN (authoritative):** Triggers a **FAILOVER** (unless there is no healthy fallback) [2].
2.  **Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity):** Triggers a **FAILOVER** or **PARTIAL_SHIFT**, depending on capacity and blast radius [2].
3.  **Tail latency burn (p99/p95):** Triggers a **PARTIAL_SHIFT** first, then escalates to **FAILOVER** if the signal is sustained and corroborated [2].
4.  **Capacity exhaustion / hard gate:** Triggers a **HOLD + load shed** (via controller action) to avoid shifting traffic into a constrained region [2].
5.  **Control plane degradation:** Triggers a **HOLD** to prevent rapid flipping and oscillation [2].

6) hold_down_active(last_flip_at, min_hold_down_seconds) -> bool
- If true, policy engine returns HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative. 7) flip_budget_ok(tenant_id, route_id, max_flips_per_hour) -> bool

- Enforces “can’t shift more than X% traffic for tier Y without approval”. - For Hosted, blast radius is route-scoped; for Dedicated, pool-scoped. B) Deterministic evaluation mode (required)

Priority order (proposed canonical order for v1):
1) Reachability DOWN (authoritative) => FAILOVER (unless no healthy fallback)
2) Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity) => FAILOVER or PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on blast radius and capacity
3) Tail latency burn (p99/p95) => PARTIAL_SHIFT first; escalate to FAILOVER if corroborated and sustained
4) Capacity exhaustion / hard gate => HOLD + load shed (controller action), avoid shifting into constrained region
5) Control plane degradation => HOLD (do not flip rapidly; prevent oscillation)

Notes:
- “No healthy fallback” means every eligible fallback region fails capacity_hard_gate OR reachability is down OR stale beyond threshold. - If no healthy fallback, decision should be HOLD and include “degrade_allowed=true” hint (controller can activate load shedding / retry-after).

========

This document captures a reproducible experiment matrix for operator-driven fallback strategies and an associated cost-penalty catalog used to evaluate trade-offs between SLO preservation and unit economics across regional surges. Intended audience: platform operators, SREs, runtime engineers, and product engineers running controlled degradation experiments or designing automatic fallback policies. Why this exists
---------------
- Fallbacks preserve SLOs during capacity scarcity or model regressions, but they can change cost, quality, and customer experience. - Operators need a concise experiment plan with metrics, dashboard queries, and a cost penalty model to compare candidate strategies. - We want a single template for telemetry, rollout/rollback steps, and decision criteria for productionizing fallbacks. Goals and scope
---------------
- Goal: Repeatable experiment matrix yielding quantitative comparisons of: latency SLO retention, token-cost delta, quality regressions (evals), and operator intervention effort. - Scope: Multiregion inference surface (hosted + dedicated), model variant fallbacks (quantized, smaller model families), routing degradations (regional drain, tenant throttling).

- **Hold-down and anti-flap timers were too permissive** for the observed signal volatility. - **Rollback semantics were correct per implementation**, but not aligned with our intended ADR-level behavior (we rolled back too quickly and re-triggered failover immediately). ## Contributing factors
### 1) Trigger noise and insufficient corroboration
- Reachability was treated as “high priority,” but we lacked a strict requirement for corroboration (e.g., simultaneous 5xx burn or control-plane health degradation) before acting. - Probe failures were short-lived and likely influenced by transient provider/network behavior; the region health pipeline did not dampen enough. ### 2) Rollback gaps / anti-flap guardrails
- Policy flip rate limiting (per policy/per tenant) was not strict enough for production-like behavior. - The controller was allowed to both:
  - fail over on a high-priority signal transition, and
  - roll back on early recovery indication,
  without a sufficiently long “stabilization” window. ### 3) Retry amplification during routing changes
- Gateway retry budgets and client retry behavior interacted poorly with redirects and timeouts. - During oscillation, some requests were retried across regions, increasing load at the exact time the target region was receiving new traffic. ### 4) Observability gaps during the test

## Overview
This page is the current internal FAQ for answering enterprise buyer questions about purchasing Redwood Inference through AWS Marketplace (public offer vs private offer), and the most common security/compliance questions (SOC 2, encryption/KMS, retention, audit logs, data residency, incident response, and SSO/RBAC). This content is used by AEs/SEs for deals where the customer prefers AWS Marketplace so spend can count toward AWS commitments (e.g., EDP) and to streamline vendor onboarding. ---

## What customers typically ask for (quick list)
- Why buy via AWS Marketplace (EDP/committed spend, consolidated invoicing) and when to use a private offer. - SKU fit: Hosted API now, Dedicated capacity later, and when Private (VPC) is required. - Metering and billing: dimensions (tokens/requests), reporting cadence, and invoice visibility. - Security questionnaire items: SOC 2 posture, encryption/KMS, retention controls, audit logs, data residency, incident response, and SSO/RBAC. - Shared responsibility boundaries for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. - Onboarding flow: subscription → entitlement validation → org provisioning/linking → first API key → first call. - Support and escalation expectations for marketplace customers. ---

## Marketplace procurement FAQ

### Q: Public offer or private offer? **Recommended for enterprise: Private offer.** Private offers allow us to align term length, committed spend constructs, and any deal-specific exhibits (e.g., security addendum, DPA references) while still using Marketplace as the procurement channel. **Public offer** (pay-as-you-go) is typically used for small pilots or when procurement does not require an order-form-like artifact. ### Q: Does Marketplace spend count toward AWS commitments (e.g., EDP)? In most enterprise cases **yes**, but eligibility is determined by the customer’s AWS agreement and how the offer is accepted. When asked, we should state:
- We structure offers using standard AWS Marketplace constructs. - The customer should confirm EDP crediting mechanics with their AWS account team.

**Customer content (MUST remain within pinned region(s))**
- Prompt / messages / input text (including system prompts provided by customer)
- Tool/function call arguments provided by customer
- Uploaded documents or retrieved passages (RAG payloads) provided by customer
- Model outputs (including partial streaming tokens)
- Embeddings input text and embeddings vectors derived from customer text

- Any debug payloads that include raw request/response bodies

**Not customer content (may be processed outside pinned region(s) under constraints below)**
- Non-content operational metadata that does not include request/response bodies and cannot reasonably be used to reconstruct them (see “Allowed cross-region metadata”). Notes:
- Whether content includes PII is not determinative; **all prompts/outputs are treated as sensitive content**. - “Derived” includes transformations (tokenization, embedding vectors, compression) if they are computed from customer text/output. ### 2) Enforcement boundary: “Where residency applies”
For pinned orgs/projects/API keys, **all handling of customer content** must remain in allowed region(s) for:
- **Request routing** and execution (including retries and fallbacks)
- **Background work** that uses the request payload or output (e.g., async logging of bodies, eval capture, replay queues)
- **Persistence and caching** of any form of request/response content
- **Observability signals** that contain content (logs/traces/debug captures)

Residency enforcement is evaluated at request time by the gateway/routing policy engine and must be **deterministic** (same policy + same request context → same allow/block outcome).

The new alerting approach reduces noise and speeds up root cause analysis (RCA) through the following mechanisms:

*   **Grouping by Stage Footprint:** Instead of per-route or per-quantile alerts, the system uses a `token_stage_cohort` service to group requests into "stage-aware cohorts" [1]. It computes a deterministic cohort key for each invocation based on stage-level metrics, such as token counts per stage, kv-cache hit patterns, and decode-batch size [1].
*   **Reducing Noise:** To prevent alert noise, the system implements an "automatic quiet-window attenuation" during its rollout [1]. Additionally, the approach aims to move away from highly granular labels (like `kernel_id` or `prompt_bucket`) which can cause hundreds of unique time series and deduplication breaks [10].
*   **Accelerating Root Cause Analysis:** 
    *   **Alert Route-Matrix:** The system introduces an alert route-matrix generator that consumes cohort rollups to emit alert bindings. These bindings are designed to "bias escalation to the top-k stages for that route," effectively attributing SLO violations to the most likely pipeline stage [1].
    *   **Specialized Dashboards:** A new dashboard is provided to help on-call engineers quickly validate root cause hypotheses by focusing on cohort drift, stage heatmaps, and per-cohort cost/latency breakdowns [1].

context_chunks.text: Context: long-tail token cost and multi-stage latency spikes frequently surface only when a request traverses several model-serving stages (tokenization, encoder, decode, fallback). Existing alerts were per-route and per-quantile but lacked a compact way to group requests by 'stage footprint' and automatically route alerting weight to the stage(s) most likely responsible. Motivation: reduce alert noise and accelerate RCA by grouping invocations into stage-aware cohorts and deriving a route x stage alert matrix that attributes SLO violations to the most likely pipeline stage. What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight token_stage_cohort service that computes a deterministic cohort key per invocation based on stage-level metrics (token counts per stage, kv-cache hit pattern, decode-batch size) and stores short-lived cohort aggregates. 2) Introduces an alert route-matrix generator that consumes cohort rollups and emits alert bindings which bias escalation to the top-k stages for that route. 3) Adds a new dashboard focused on cohort drift, stage heatmaps, and per-cohort cost/latency breakdown to help oncall quickly validate root cause hypotheses. 4) Wires the generator into the existing alerting pipeline with a safe canary rollout and automatic quiet-window attenuation to avoid regressing noise. Compatibility and rollout: service defaults to read-only mode until flagged by a feature flag; alert generation starts cross-account in a low-sensitivity mode (only P90/P99) and is then ramped after 72h of monitoring. Testing: unit and integration tests added; ran a 48h synthetic replay against production-like traces (see test run in CI). Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Dashboard panels - [x] Docs for oncall and runbook - [x] Feature-flagged rollout Plan for operators: deploy to staging -> enable feature flag -> monitor cohort drift and false-positive rate -> bump sensitivity -> full rollout. Summary

This page documents a repeatable, instructor-led bootcamp to train platform operators and engineers to write high-quality runbooks that are telemetry-driven, testable, and maintainable. The curriculum is designed for new operators, service owners, and incident responders who will author or own runbooks for platform services (prefix cache, allocator, tenant-slicing, model-variant router). Audience

- Platform operators and SREs
- Service owners in eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime
- Oncall engineers who respond to latency/cost incidents

Learning objectives (measurable)

1. Produce a runbook that contains a clear escalation path, data-driven detection predicates, and an operator checklist. 2. Write two telemetry queries (one metric-based, one log-based) that reliably surface the condition the runbook describes. 3. Create a synthetic verification (unit) that validates the runbook’s detection predicates against a small replay dataset. 4. Implement a post-incident update cycle and link to the action in the runbook so it can be closed by the owner. Curriculum overview (3-day instructor-led)

Day 0 — Prework (self-paced)
- Read: "Runbook authoring and maintenance guidelines" (required). - Complete a short quiz on SLO definitions and common platform failure modes. - Setup: access to Grafana/Tempo, Kibana, and a sandbox tenant. Confirm permissions with infra-oncall. Day 1 — Foundations and detection
- Morning: Lecture (1.5 hr) — Runbook structure and the telemetry-first principle. - Sections: Summary, Impact, Detection (metric + log predicates), Immediate actions, Escalation, Rollback, Postmortem link. - Example services: kv-prefix-cache, dynamic-allocator, model-variant-router. - Lab (2.5 hr): Write detection predicates for a synthetic latency spike:
  1) Metric predicate: p95 latency > 300ms for 5m AND error rate > 1% for 2m. 2) Log predicate: queries that include "kv-cache:miss" and "eviction-reason=reshuffle" for >50 events in 10m. - Homework: Author a first draft runbook for a provided scenario.

- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies). - Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues. - Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers. Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

The root cause was identified as a known bridging bug in the switch firmware (version 1.2.3) [3]. Specifically, the switch's **'proxy-arp' feature** was injecting gratuitous ARP replies for VPN client IPs whenever the AP's multicast queue exceeded a certain threshold (70%) [3].

This caused the switch to return ARP replies for the same IP using a different MAC address that matched a spare management interface in rack 7 (00:66:77:88:99:AA) [3]. This resulted in the observed duplicate IP warnings and intermittent VPN connectivity blackholes (lasting 30-90s) for users on the 'Redwood-Corp' Wi-Fi behind the edge switch (edge-sw-7) in the SF2 building [2, 3].

context_chunks.text: Issue summary: After a recent office CAB change at the SoMa satellite office we started seeing a sustained increase in VPN session failures and SSO timeouts for users on the office Wi‑Fi. Impact: ~12-18% of users at SoMa experience intermittent 403/SSO timeouts or are unable to reach internal services that normally resolve via VPN private IPs. Service impact is localized to the office LAN and affects employees using company Wi‑Fi and a subset of developer services behind policy-based routing. Initial hypothesis: an intermediate bridge/AP that was re-provisioned to 'NAT' mode is rewriting source addresses causing VPN policy lookup to fail, triggering mis-routed traffic and SSO token validation errors. 1) Connect a laptop to SoMa corporate Wi‑Fi (ssid: Redwood-Corp). 2) Establish Redwood VPN (WireGuard client) and authenticate via SSO (Okta). 3) Attempt to curl an internal service at 10.11.20.5: expect success; observed: connection resets or 403 responses. 4) Observe device local IP (e.g., 192.168.50.34) and the outbound NATed IP as seen by internal services (packets show 10.100.200.1 source after NAT rewrite). Clients on office Wi‑Fi see internal service requests fail intermittently. Packet captures from service frontends show source IPs mapped to 10.100.200.0/24 (bridge appliance SNAT pool) instead of clients' VPN-assigned 10.8.0.0/16 addresses. Okta SSO validation rejects token assertions when source IP does not match expected corporate ranges, causing auth flows to fail. Traffic from VPN clients should preserve VPN-assigned source addresses. Office bridge should be in passthrough mode for tunneled traffic so policy-based routing at the gateway can correctly match flows and SSO sees expected IP ranges.

Summary:
This document describes a recurring class of production incidents we term 'ingress proxy connection entropy' that manifest as intermittent 502/503/504 errors and short spikes of failed model fanout requests. It provides:

- clear symptom definitions and diagnostic queries
- an immediate mitigation runbook for oncall and customer success engineers
- long‑term engineering fixes and rollout guidance
- test and verification checklists for customer-facing cutovers

Scope:
Applies to: Redwood-hosted ingress proxies and customer-managed sidecar proxies that perform request fanout to model serving pools (Hosted, Dedicated, Private).

Use the template 'slo-incident-summary' and attach trace artifacts.

Appendix A — example CLI and config snippets:

1) Quick sysctl hotfix (Linux):
```
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_limit=50
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=2048
```

2) Routing override to reduce fanout (routing-cli sample):
```
routing-cli set-fanout --route tenant:acme/chat --mode sequential --max-variants 2 --reason "mitigating connection entropy"
```

3) Nginx/TCP proxy snippet (increase backlog / keepalive):
```
worker_processes auto;
events { worker_connections  65536; }
stream {
  server {
    listen 443 backlog=2048 reuseport;
    proxy_pass backend_pool;
    proxy_timeout 65s;
    proxy_connect_timeout 10s;
  }
}
```

- pcap capture from affected proxy (90s)
- higher-sample traces (25%) for 2 hours

The recommended two-stage process for rotating signing credentials is a two-phase operation consisting of a **Preflight** phase and a **Cutover** phase [1, 2].

### **Phase A: Preflight (No Live Swap)**
The goal of this phase is to test the new credentials without affecting the live environment [1].
1.  **Provisioning:** Provision a new KMS key version and create an alias (`kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN`) [1].
2.  **Deployment:** Deploy CI adapters (`sign-image-action`) to use the new key (`key-vN`) in a feature-flagged mode [1].
3.  **Testing:** Run 100% test-signings that do not change the promotion ledger and verify that attestation services accept the new signatures [1].
4.  **Shadow Copy:** Run a shadow cross-account copy using an ephemeral role with the new signing metadata to confirm successful copies across all target regions [1].
5.  **Monitoring:** Monitor for 24 hours (or 3 release windows) to check for any unexpected pull authentication regressions [1].

### **Phase B: Cutover (The Swap)**
This phase executes the actual transition to the new credentials [1].
1.  **Scheduling:** Schedule a change window with a target Service Level Objective (SLO) of less than 30 minutes of "blind window" [1].
2.  **Atomic Swap:** Perform an atomic alias swap to update `kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN` [1].
3.  **Revocation:** After a 5-minute grace period, revoke the short-lived CI credentials associated with the previous key (`key-vN-1`) and rotate ephemeral role sessions [1].
4.  **Canary Promotion:** Promote a single canary image signed with the new key (`key-vN`) and verify its health across latency and error metrics for 20 minutes [1].
5.  **Full Rollout:** If no triggers are fired during the canary phase, proceed to full fleet promotion [1].

### **How to Roll Back**
The process includes both automated and manual rollback procedures depending on the failure type:

*   **During Cutover:** If triggers are fired during the canary phase, revert the alias back to the previous key (`key-vN-1`) and mark the new key (`key-vN`) as "revocation-pending" for forensic review [1].
*   **Automated Rollbacks (Based on Safety Matrix):**
    *   **Canary Latency:** If the 99th percentile latency increases by >40% vs baseline, the system can auto-revert to the previous tag in 15 minutes if more than two buckets exceed the threshold [2].
    *   **Error Rates:** If 5xx error rates exceed 0.5% absolute, the system should abort promotion; if the error persists for 10 minutes, a full fleet rollback is triggered [2].
    *   **Pull Auth Errors:** If pull authentication errors are $\ge$ 3% across $\ge$ 2 regions and persist for 10 minutes, an automated rollback and revocation of the ephemeral role is performed [2].
*   **Manual/Immediate Actions:**
    *   **Signature Mismatches:** If an image signature mismatch is reported, the specific image tag should be quarantined by marking it as "blocked" in the promotion ledger [1, 2].
    *   **Tokenization Errors:** Any runtime error in tokenization requires a manual rollback after investigation [2].

Emergency rollback runbook (oncall steps)
1) Detect: Pager fires for pull auth failures or mass pod CrashLoopBackOff when pulling prod images. 2) Immediate action (within first 5 minutes):
   - Confirm via cross-region registry metrics whether pull auth errors are present and their percentage. - If pull auth failures >=3% across >=2 regions, run: ./scripts/revoke-ci-ephemeral-sessions --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-ephemeral-publisher
   - If image signature mismatch reported, quarantine the image tag: mark in the promotion ledger as blocked.

Safety principles (high level)
1) Always sign images with key versioning (KMS key alias + key-id). Verification must include key version metadata. 2) Use a promotion plan that stages in-region canaries before full fleet promotion. 3) Make credential rotation a two-phase operation: preflight (test) then swap (cutover) with automatic rollback on failure. 4) Prefer short-lived credentials (ephemeral IAM role / signed cert) for CI agents; store long-term secrets only in HSM-backed KMS. 5) Maintain an explicit PROMOTION SAFETY MATRIX mapping signals to actions (below). Promotion safety matrix\
| Signal | Threshold | Action | Rollback trigger |
|--------|-----------:|--------|-----------------|
| Canary 99th latency increase | +40% vs baseline | Halt promotion, mark image suspect, run deeper perf trace | Auto-revert to previous tag in 15m if >2 buckets exceed threshold |
| Error rate (5xx) | >0.5% absolute | Re-route 100% traffic off canary nodes, abort promotion | Full fleet rollback if persisted for 10m |
| Tokenization mismatch (new tokenizer failure) | any runtime error | Halt; capture failing prompt, block image | Manual rollback after investigation |
| Image signature verification failures | any | Stop promotion, alert security, revoke CI key version | Block until signature chain validated |
| Pull auth errors across >=2 regions | >=3% pull failures | Pause promotion; force ephemeral credential refresh | If persists 10m, automated rollback and revoke ephemeral role |

Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

- runtime_image: redwood/runtime-infer:2025-10-21

- concurrency_profile: \"single-req\" | \"batched\"

Overview
=======

Purpose: This playbook consolidates company-wide procedures for entitlements (access and permissions), change governance, data handling expectations, procurement and expense approvals, vendor lifecycle management, and travel approvals. It is intended for all Redwood employees and contractors who request or approve resources, commit changes to production, or manage third-party relationships. Scope: Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment teams, platform and infra teams, procurement interactions, people-ops travel arrangements, and any third party that will access Redwood systems or customer data. Quick links: Access Portal (Okta + Access Request), VendorHub (procurement back-end), ExpenseFlow (employee expenses), Legal intake form, Security questionnaire (security.redwood.local). Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------

- Requestor: person initiating an access, change, purchase, vendor relationship, or travel booking. Responsible for completeness and business justification. - Manager/Approver: direct manager who validates business need and budget availability. - Approving Officer (Finance/Procurement): validates procurement thresholds, tax, and vendor classification. - Security Reviewer: evaluates data access risk and mandatory controls (SOC2, encryption, contract clauses). - Legal Reviewer: reviews contract terms for vendor agreements above threshold or with custom IP/data terms. - Proc Ops (Vendor Onboarding): completes supplier setup, obtains W-9/COI as applicable. Principles
----------

- Least privilege: grant minimal entitlements required for the job and set automatic expiration where practical. - Segregation of duties: approval and provisioning paths must not be owned by the same individual for medium/high risk requests. - Evidence-first approvals: all approvals must be attached to the request in VendorHub or Access Portal. - Risk proportionality: stricter controls for vendors with data access, privileged infra access, or requests above financial thresholds.

Cost calculations (short formulas)
- token_cost_delta_hourly = sum_over_requests(token_count * (cost_primary - cost_fallback)) per hour
- egress_delta_hourly = egress_bytes * egress_rate
- revenue_at_risk = blocked_requests * avg_revenue_per_request

For the incident involving KV cache "ghost" entries (caused by negative refcounts), the metric name added for counting these increments is **"negative-refcount increments"** [1, 3].

The incident documentation specifies that there should be "No new negative-refcount increments in metrics for 72h after full rollout" to verify the fix [3].

context_chunks.text: Summary: During a capacity surge on 2025-11-08 we observed a slow but persistent memory growth on several serving nodes which culminated in degraded tail latency and two short-lived OOMs. Investigation showed a new class of 'ghost' entries in the KV prefix cache: entries whose refcount had decayed below zero (underflow) due to an interaction between async compaction, prefetch migration, and a recent refcount optimization. These ghost entries never surfaced as normal cache misses and therefore were not collected by the existing eviction heuristics, leading to gradual slab exhaustion on hot shards. This ticket captures detection heuristics, an emergency snapshot sanitization runbook, a staged rolling-heal design (scheduled drains + isolated snapshot rewrite), telemetry improvements, and a rollout/verification plan. Memory growth first seen 2025-11-06, customer latency degradation at p95/p99 experienced across dedicated and hosted clusters on 2025-11-08. Two nodes hit transient OOMs and auto-recovered (restarts). No persistent data loss; customer requests were served with fallbacks but experienced elevated errors and higher per-token latency. Estimated affected capacity 8% of serving fleet during surge window. Concurrency bug: an optimization in the refcount update path batched decrement operations to reduce atomic ops. Under a race where async compaction rewrites slab bitmaps concurrently with prefetch migrators moving KV records across buckets, the batched decrement could be applied twice for the same logical record. This produced negative refcounts and left entries in an invisible 'ghost' state that bypassed eviction score updates. Compaction also left behind partial tombstone metadata which confused the slab reclaim heuristics. A1: Emergency snapshot sanitization script - implement and run a conservative scanner to detect negative refcounts and mark entries for reclamation. Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2025-11-18.

Specifically, reprovisioning the device on 2026-03-09 set its WAN mode to 'Gateway (NAT)', which enabled SNAT (Source Network Address Translation) [1]. Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["

", "


"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust.

## Summary
On **2026-01-15**, during a **planned controlled regional failover test** (Hosted API and a limited Dedicated slice) from **us-east** to **eu-west**, we introduced a **customer-visible regression**. A sequence of noisy regional-impairment signals and insufficient rollback/anti-flap guardrails caused repeated routing policy changes (“flip/rollback”) and a transient overload condition in the target region. **Customer impact:**
- **Hosted API:** elevated 5xx/timeouts and tail latency for a subset of routes while traffic re-converged. - **Dedicated:** minimal direct impact due to scoped tenants, but some control-plane operations (drain workflow status) were delayed. - **Streaming:** some clients experienced disconnects on redirect and did not recover cleanly without application-level retries. **Why this postmortem exists:** This was an intentional test. The regression was not catastrophic, but it was **customer-visible** and exposed gaps in our automation safety model. The goal is to make sure controlled testing improves reliability without creating new incidents. ## Severity and scope
- **Incident type:** Planned test causing unplanned customer-visible regression
- **Severity:** SEV-2 (customer-visible errors for a limited subset; short duration; mitigated quickly)
- **Services impacted:** Hosted API (gateway + smart routing), failover automation controller, region health evaluation pipeline
- **Regions:** us-east (source), eu-west (target)

## Customer impact (what users experienced)
- Transient **HTTP 5xx** and **gateway timeouts** during the flip/rollback window. - Elevated **p95/p99 latency** for successful requests during the same interval. - Some **streaming sessions** dropped when redirected cross-region; a subset of clients did not resume streaming until they retried from the application. Notes:
- We did not publish an external status page incident because this was a planned test with limited blast radius; however, **Support received inbound tickets** from customers who noticed errors during the window.

The root cause of the February 12, 2026, incident was a **deduplication bug** in the usage exporter, which treated retried streaming chunks as distinct completions when a request ID changed across retry boundaries [1].

To address the incident, the following steps were taken:

**Mitigation**
*   The team **paused export generation** and then performed a **backfill** after the fix was implemented [1].
*   The export logic was updated, and exports resumed with **corrected logic** [1].

**Follow-up Action Items**
To prevent a repeat of the issue, three specific action items were identified:
1.  **Add a reconciliation job** that compares the invoice counter against the export counter per workspace per day, triggering a page if the drift is greater than 0.5% [1].
2.  **Fix the usage exporter deduplication logic** to ensure it uses a stable trace ID across retries [1].
3.  **Add a contract test** in the usage pipeline specifically for streaming retry semantics [1].

answer:
The underlying parsing problem was that the `groups` SAML attribute contained a leading **UTF-8 BOM** (Byte Order Mark) with the hex values `0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF` [1]. While the server's group-splitting routine used `strings.Split` on a comma and then `TrimSpace`, this process removed whitespace but failed to remove the leading BOM [2]. Consequently, the first group name in the CSV string appeared to be empty or mismatched because it was prefixed with the BOM, preventing it from matching the expected role mapping (e.g., `crestline-admins`) [1, 2].

The issue was fixed with a server-side patch that implemented a **`NormalizeUnicode`** function to strip the BOM and control characters from the attribute values before the splitting process occurred [2].

Customer reported that after onboarding to Private VPC (prod-us-east) a subset of their admin users suddenly lost admin privileges and received 403s from the Admin Console APIs. The customers use a SAML IdP (OnPrem SAML 2.0) that sends a 'groups' SAML attribute exported as a single CSV string containing group names. Impact:
- Multiple tenant admins unable to perform admin actions (create API keys, manage billing, role bindings)
- Affects ~6 user accounts in Crestline Analytics (customer-declared admins)
- Production (prod-us-east) only; no impact observed in staging. Environment:
- Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane) deployed in VPC (us-east-1)
- SAML SSO via customer's IdP (SAMLResponse sent to /auth/saml/acs)
- Role mapping configured: first matching group name -> Admin role

Steps to reproduce (as reported):
1) User signs in via SAML SSO. 2) Authn completes and SAMLResponse posted to our ACS. 3) User attempts an admin API call (create api-key). 4) Received 403 Forbidden from Admin API. Observed behavior:
- Successful authentication (session created), but RBAC mapping does not include the expected 'crestline-admins' group for affected users. - Server-side logs show groups attribute present but first group value appears empty when parsed by our role-mapper. Example raw attribute (hex): "EF BB BF 63 72 65 73 74 6C 69 6E 65 2D 61 64 6D 69 6E 73,..." which corresponds to a leading UTF-8 BOM (0xEF,0xBB,0xBF) before 'crestline-admins'. Expected behavior:
- All groups listed in the SAML attribute should be parsed and matched against role mapping rules; admin users should receive the Admin role. Temporary workaround recommended to customer:
- Add a secondary mapping that matches the literal BOM-prefixed group (not ideal). - Alternatively, configure IdP to strip/normalize attribute values prior to assertion export. Notes:
- Customer confirmed IdP was recently upgraded and exported group values using a library that appears to inject a leading BOM on some exports (particularly from their Windows-based AD connector).

- Alternatively, configure IdP to strip/normalize attribute values prior to assertion export. Notes:
- Customer confirmed IdP was recently upgraded and exported group values using a library that appears to inject a leading BOM on some exports (particularly from their Windows-based AD connector). - This behavior only affects assertions coming from that connector; other users (federated via Okta) are unaffected. [2026-03-10 14:28 UTC] Arjun Patel (Auth Eng): Confirmed raw base64-decode of SAMLResponse shows groups attribute beginning with bytes EF BB BF. Hypothesis: leading UTF-8 BOM present, parser trims whitespace but not BOM. Adding instrumentation to log hex of first bytes for affected assertions. [2026-03-11 02:03 UTC] SRE (Priya Nair): Deployed temporary logging change to private control plane to capture raw attribute bytes for a short window. No other customer affected during window. [2026-03-11 08:47 UTC] Arjun Patel (Auth Eng): Reproduced locally by injecting BOM into groups attribute. Our group-splitting routine uses strings.Split on comma and then TrimSpace, which does not remove the BOM. Created patch to run NormalizeUnicode(strip BOM and control chars) on attribute values before splitting. [2026-03-12 10:21 UTC] Customer: Confirmed patch rollout to their private cluster restored admin role for previously affected users. No further 403s observed for those accounts. [2026-03-12 15:30 UTC] Maya Chen (Support): Marking as resolved-pending follow-up. Customer asks for guidance to prevent recurrence; provided runbook entry and suggested IdP config adjustments. Reproduction: Created test SAMLResponse with groups='\uFEFFcrestline-admins,developers' and posted to ACS.

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 403s for users immediately after the IdP (On-prem SAML IdP) performs a group sync. Impact: Admin and write operations are blocked for some users while they can still view resources. Occurs only in Nimbus Health's private deployment (prod-us-east) and started after their nightly group-sync job. Environment: private deployment (VPC) with SSO proxied through our identity-proxy; session cookies used are SameSite=Lax, cookie named rwd_sess. Customer performed an IdP-side role changeset at 03:40 UTC and ran group sync. Symptoms observed for ~seconds-to-minutes window: some affected users receive 403s for actions requiring newly granted roles while others (or same users after logout/login) succeed. Observed severity: P1 due to business-impacting admin ops during business hours. 1) Customer updates group->role mapping on IdP and triggers IdP group sync. 2) User with existing browser session performs an admin API call (e.g., POST /v1/admin/projects/:id/keys). 3) Server responds 403 with rbac denial. 4) If user logs out and logs back in, call succeeds. Repro rate: intermittent but correlated with IdP sync events. [2026-03-10T03:41:02Z] auth:rbac deny user=uid:94e3 session_index=sess-0a7f reason='no-matching-role-after-eval' path=/v1/admin/projects/42/members status=403 request_id=aa7b2c
[2026-03-10T03:41:03Z] sso:proxy debug session_lookup key=sess-0a7f -> cache HIT ttl=18s roles=[team:viewer]
[2026-03-10T03:41:05Z] idp-notify info received user-change webhook for uid:94e3 groups=[prod-admins]
[2026-03-10T03:41:07Z] auth:rbac eval user=uid:94e3 live-lookup roles=[team:admin] result=ALLOW

03/10 05:45 UTC - Customer provided request logs and IdP group sync trace. Confirmed 403 responses followed immediately after IdP sync events. Hypothesis: identity-proxy caches role assertions keyed by SAML session_index for performance; when IdP updates groups, existing sessions still return the cached role set until cache expiry.

Issue summary: Atlas Retail observed that several service accounts and a subset of human users were granted admin-level routes in their private VPC deployment despite RBAC policies that should exclude them via a 'not_in' expression. Impact: Incorrectly permissive access to admin/config APIs for a small number of identities, risk of configuration changes. Environment: Private deployment (customer-managed control plane), prod-us-east region, customer using SSO via their IdP with claims delivered as JWT to the identity-proxy. Observation window: 2026-03-12 22:30 - 2026-03-13 03:00 UTC. Steps to reproduce: 1) Customer provided a minimal policy that allows action if user.entitlements not_in ["admin", "superuser"] 2) Send request with JWT that omits the 'entitlements' claim altogether 3) Call to /admin/config returns 200 and allowed instead of denied. Expected behavior: Missing claim should be treated as empty set and 'not_in' should evaluate to true for empty set only if semantics intended; policy author expected deny when admin exclusion is required. Observed behavior: Policy evaluator treats missing claim in 'not_in' as a non-match that bypasses exclusion, resulting in grant. Customer impact: Two internal teams escalated (SRE and Platform) and temporarily halted config pushes. No data exfiltration detected.

To address p99 latency spikes correlated with KV compaction in Runtime 1.22 on Hosted (Shared) pools, oncall should take the following actions:

**Knobs to Tune First**
The two knobs to tune first (in order of recommendation) are:
1.  **`kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step`**: Reduce this by **25–50%** [3, 4].
2.  **`kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step`**: Reduce this by **25–50%** [3, 4].

**Emergency Kill-Switch**
The emergency kill-switch to disable compaction (pool-scoped) is to set:
*   **`kv.compaction.enabled=false`** [3]

**Verification of Disable**
To confirm the disable took effect, check the following:
*   **Metrics:** Confirm metrics show the expected directional change, specifically a **lower compaction time** (e.g., lower `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` growth) [3, 4].
*   **Config Propagation:** Confirm that the fleet shows the **new effective config** within 10 minutes of the change [4].

## Summary
Runtime 1.22 introduces **KV cache compaction** and **tier-aware KV eviction** to reduce GPU memory fragmentation and mitigate burst-driven tail latency (p95/p99) for sustained decode workloads with mixed sequence lengths. This release adds:
- A **fragmentation-aware allocator health model** (new fragmentation metrics and allocator state tracking). - **Budgeted compaction** (time/bytes) integrated with the scheduler to avoid decode stalls. - A **tier-aware eviction policy** (LRU-by-sequence with safety constraints) to prevent opportunistic/chaotic evictions during bursts. - **Tracing spans and exemplars** to correlate compaction/eviction events with tail latency. - A **kill-switch** and rollout knobs to allow oncall to disable compaction/eviction quickly. Primary expected impact:
- Lower tail latency variance during bursts and churn. - Reduced incidence of “allocator thrash” and fragmentation-driven OOM/forced shedding. - Minimal steady-state throughput impact when budgets are respected. ---

## Who is impacted
**Internal:** Runtime, SRE, Release Engineering, Support, Solutions/CS, Product (Hosted + Dedicated). **External:** Customers on Hosted and Dedicated tiers (and Private if enabled by the account/cluster owner). There are no API surface changes; behavior changes are limited to runtime memory management under load. ---

## What changed (high-level)
### 1) Compaction (new)
The runtime can now **relocate KV pages** to increase contiguity in the KV arena when fragmentation exceeds a trigger threshold. Compaction is incremental and budgeted to limit latency impact. Key properties:
- **Budgeted per scheduler phase** to avoid decode stalls (see “Default settings by tier”). - Uses safe stopping conditions; compaction yields when latency-sensitive work is queued. - Relocation is tracked with counters + traces; correctness is validated under cancellation/churn scenarios.

|
| Private (VPC / On-prem) | OFF (default) | OFF (default) | Must be enabled per cluster after validating observability + headroom; recommended for bursty multi-tenant private clusters. |

### Runtime flags (names + intended meaning)
The following flags are referenced in docs/runbooks; exact propagation is via runtime config profiles. - `kv.compaction.enabled` (bool)
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio` (float 0..1)
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step` (int)
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step` (int)
- `kv.compaction.max_steps_per_tick` (int)
- `kv.eviction.enabled` (bool)
- `kv.eviction.policy` (string; default: `tier_aware_lru`)
- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target` (int)
- `kv.eviction.protect_pinned_sessions` (bool; default: true)
- `kv.kill_switch` (bool; emergency disable compaction+eviction)

### Recommended defaults (current Runtime 1.22 release train)
Hosted (Shared):
- `kv.compaction.enabled = true`
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio = 0.30`
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step = 2`
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step = 268435456` (256 MiB)
- `kv.compaction.max_steps_per_tick = 1`
- `kv.eviction.enabled = true`
- `kv.eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru`
- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target = 1073741824` (1 GiB)
- `kv.kill_switch = false`

Dedicated:
- `kv.compaction.enabled = true`
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio = 0.35`
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step = 3`
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step = 402653184` (384 MiB)
- `kv.compaction.max_steps_per_tick = 1`
- `kv.eviction.enabled = true`
- `kv.eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru`
- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target = 536870912` (512 MiB)
- `kv.kill_switch = false`

Private (VPC / On-prem):
- `kv.compaction.enabled = false` (default)
- `kv.eviction.enabled = false` (default)
- If enabling: start with Hosted-like budgets and confirm dashboards/alerts are wired (see Monitoring). Why these defaults:
- Lower trigger ratios + strict budgets reduce the chance of compaction clustering into noticeable latency spikes.

### Red flags
- Fragmentation ratio trending upward with **flat** compaction activity (trigger not met, disabled, or worker stuck). - High `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` growth accompanied by p99 latency spikes (budget too high or running at bad scheduler phase). - Sudden increase in `kv_alloc_failures_total` or OOM events while fragmentation is high (eviction not engaging / min-free target too low). - Non-zero `kv_evictions_blocked_total{reason=pinned}` followed by evictions from pinned sessions (bug / configuration regression). ---

## Common incidents and how to respond

### 1) Tail latency spike (p95/p99) correlated with compaction
**Symptoms**
- `request_latency_ms_p99` increases within 5–15 minutes of enabling compaction on a canary cohort. - `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` slope increases sharply. - Traces show long `kv.compaction.step` spans near decode. **Immediate actions (least risky first)**
1) Reduce compaction budget:
   - Lower `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step` by 25–50% OR
   - Lower `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step` by 25–50%
2) Ensure compaction runs at safe scheduler boundaries:
   - Prefer `mode=scheduler_hook` or `hybrid` with strict decode gating in Hosted pools. 3) Raise the trigger threshold slightly if compaction is engaging too early:
   - Increase `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio` by +0.03 to +0.05

**If p99 remains elevated for >10 minutes**
- Disable compaction for the canary cohort (keep eviction enabled if safe):
  - Set `kv.compaction.enabled=false` (pool-scoped)
- Follow the rollout rollback criteria (see SRE guardrails page). **Notes**
- Do not over-correct budgets to zero; you can worsen fragmentation and trigger allocator pressure later in the day.

### Recommended knobs (in order)
1) `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step`
2) `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step`
3) `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio`
4) `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target`

### Example: reduce compaction impact during canary
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step=2`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step=33554432`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config apply --pool <POOL_NAME>`

### Example: enable eviction as an OOM guardrail
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.eviction.enabled=true`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.eviction.policy=tier_aware_lru`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target=2147483648`
- `redwoodctl runtime-config apply --pool <POOL_NAME>`

### Validation after a change (required)
Within 10 minutes of apply:
- Confirm config propagation completed (fleet shows new effective config)
- Confirm metrics show expected directional change (e.g., lower compaction time)
- Confirm p99 has stabilized or improved

---

## Kill-switch and rollback procedure
Use this when:
- Canary breaches rollback criteria (tail latency, error rate, or allocator health)
- Correctness signals fire
- You cannot stabilize within the incident SLA window

### A) Kill-switch (pool-scoped)
1) Disable compaction:
   - `redwoodctl runtime-config set --pool <POOL_NAME> kv.compaction.enabled=false`
2) Decide on eviction:
   - If OOM risk is low: `kv.eviction.enabled=false`
   - If OOM risk is high: keep eviction enabled but reduce aggressiveness (lower min-free target) and monitor
3) Apply:
   - `redwoodctl runtime-config apply --pool <POOL_NAME>`

### B) Rollback the canary cohort
Follow release train policy for runtime-1.22:
1) Remove pool from canary cohort (rollout system) OR shift traffic weight to previous runtime version. 2) Confirm traffic drains. 3) Confirm p99 and allocator signals return to baseline.

The Interactive Latency Canvas is a comprehensive monitoring dashboard used by SREs, Runtime engineers, and Product Owners to compare latency across models and API routes. It features specialized panels including a latency skyline, streaming inspector, cohort analysis, and trace links for root-cause drilldowns. The dashboard enables detailed performance decomposition between streaming and blocking IO modes and provides granular control via model version and route name selectors.

The production `perf-canary` paging storm on 2026-02-12 was caused by an alerting and observability failure following the expansion of canary coverage (from 3 to 8 models in `us-east`) and the enablement of paging rules [3, 4].

**Causes:**
The incident was driven by two primary technical issues [3]:
* **Metric label cardinality inflation:** The introduction of high-cardinality labels (such as `kernel_id` and `prompt_bucket`) fragmented the canary's time series [2, 3]. This created many "small-N" series, causing the regression evaluator to oscillate between having enough and not enough samples to trigger an alert [4].
* **Baseline drift and key mismatch:** A mismatch between the canary's emitted metric labels and the baseline store's lookup key (which expected `model + model_version + sku [+region optional]`) caused frequent "baseline not found" errors [2, 3]. This forced the evaluator to fall back to default or zeroed baseline values, resulting in false-positive regressions [3, 4].
* **Deduplication failure:** The `incident-bot` dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for dimensions like `runtime_build`, causing the same underlying symptom to create repeated parallel threads and pages [4].

**Immediate Mitigations and Config Changes:**
To stop the repeated pages, the following actions were taken [2, 4]:
* **Silence/Muting:** Rafael Mendes applied a global silence in Alertmanager for `perf-canary-*page*` rules for a duration of one hour [2].
* **Disabling Rules:** SREs disabled the paging rules (while keeping warnings active) and increased the dampening window [4].
* **Rollback:** The canary configuration was rolled back to the previous 3-model set, which successfully dropped the alert volume [4].

## Summary
On 2026-02-12, the production performance canary generated a burst of false-positive alerts across multiple models and regions shortly after enabling warning + paging rules in the first expansion beyond the initial 2-model rollout. Alerts were high volume (warning + paging) and repeatedly reopened due to dedupe failures, resulting in on-call interruption and a temporary release freeze request. There was **no confirmed customer-facing latency regression** attributable to this incident. The event was an alerting/observability failure caused primarily by (1) **baseline drift + baseline key mismatch** and (2) **metric label cardinality inflation** that fragmented the canary’s time series, defeating min-sample gating and dedupe. ## Impact
### Customer impact
- **None confirmed.** Runtime and customer SLO dashboards did not show correlated sustained p95 latency increases for customer traffic. ### Internal impact
- **Paging noise:** 19 paging alerts over ~38 minutes (with multiple re-pages due to missing dedupe keys). - **Warning noise:** 60+ warning alerts over ~75 minutes. - **Operational disruption:** SRE on-call and runtime on-call diverted to triage; release engineering requested a short freeze while signals stabilized. - **Confidence impact:** Reduced trust in the perf canary as a rollout gate until remediations were in place. ### Services/systems involved
- perf-canary service (prod)
- observability-pack alert rules + Grafana dashboards
- baseline store + baseline fetch client
- telemetry pipeline (metrics ingestion + aggregation)
- incident-bot alert handler

The canary’s regression evaluator compared observed p95 latency/tokens-sec against per-model baselines. After model expansion:
- Many evaluations used **fallback baseline values** because the baseline lookup key did not match (baseline existed under a different dimension set). - Metric series were fragmented by high-cardinality labels; the regression evaluator saw many “small-N” series and oscillated between “enough samples” and “not enough samples” depending on which series was queried. - Alert rules did not consistently enforce **minimum sample size across the same grouping** used by the evaluator, which allowed small, noisy slices to trip thresholds. - incident-bot dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for (model, version, region, sku, runtime_build), so the same underlying symptom created repeated threads/pages.

The underlying cause of the Feb 2026 SEV-2 incident was a refactor in the `autoscalermetrics` PromQL query that switched label matching from `cluster_id` to `cluster` [1]. Because some clusters emitted only the `cluster_id` label, the query returned an empty series for a subset of clusters, which prevented the Dedicated autoscaler in us-west from making scale-out decisions [1].

The scale-out was restored by applying a hotfix to the autoscaler query that restored label compatibility and added a fallback query for when no series are returned [1].

In a private VPC deployment using SSO via the identity-proxy, the intermittent 403 RBAC denials were caused by the **identity-proxy caching role assertions** keyed by the SAML `session_index` for performance [1]. When the IdP performed a group sync, the `session_index` remained stable, meaning the cached entries were not invalidated; consequently, existing sessions continued to return the **stale cached role set** until the cache expired [1, 2].

The following solutions were applied:
*   **Mitigation:** Adding an immediate cache eviction upon receiving IdP `user-change` webhooks for the affected user or `session_index` [2].
*   **Long-term server-side fix:** While the provided text describes the mitigation of adding cache eviction [2], it notes that the 403s were "fixed by logging out/in" as a manual workaround for users [1]. (Note: While other documents mention different long-term fixes for different issues, for this specific identity-proxy caching issue, the SRE proposed the cache eviction on webhooks as the primary fix [2]).

Issue summary:
Customer reported that after onboarding to Private VPC (prod-us-east) a subset of their admin users suddenly lost admin privileges and received 403s from the Admin Console APIs. The customers use a SAML IdP (OnPrem SAML 2.0) that sends a 'groups' SAML attribute exported as a single CSV string containing group names. Impact:
- Multiple tenant admins unable to perform admin actions (create API keys, manage billing, role bindings)
- Affects ~6 user accounts in Crestline Analytics (customer-declared admins)
- Production (prod-us-east) only; no impact observed in staging. Environment:
- Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane) deployed in VPC (us-east-1)
- SAML SSO via customer's IdP (SAMLResponse sent to /auth/saml/acs)
- Role mapping configured: first matching group name -> Admin role

Steps to reproduce (as reported):
1) User signs in via SAML SSO. 2) Authn completes and SAMLResponse posted to our ACS. 3) User attempts an admin API call (create api-key). 4) Received 403 Forbidden from Admin API. Observed behavior:
- Successful authentication (session created), but RBAC mapping does not include the expected 'crestline-admins' group for affected users. - Server-side logs show groups attribute present but first group value appears empty when parsed by our role-mapper. Example raw attribute (hex): "EF BB BF 63 72 65 73 74 6C 69 6E 65 2D 61 64 6D 69 6E 73,..." which corresponds to a leading UTF-8 BOM (0xEF,0xBB,0xBF) before 'crestline-admins'. Expected behavior:
- All groups listed in the SAML attribute should be parsed and matched against role mapping rules; admin users should receive the Admin role. Temporary workaround recommended to customer:
- Add a secondary mapping that matches the literal BOM-prefixed group (not ideal). - Alternatively, configure IdP to strip/normalize attribute values prior to assertion export. Notes:
- Customer confirmed IdP was recently upgraded and exported group values using a library that appears to inject a leading BOM on some exports (particularly from their Windows-based AD connector).

Diego Morales (SRE): Opened INT-4456 to track rollout/patch automation for private deployments. Requested canary rollout to dedicated infra before pushing to private updater. Summary: AuthZ engine's expression runtime performs 'not_in' by iterating subject values and checking membership against target list; when claim is absent the evaluator treats subject as a single empty string value leading to membership checks that return false and overall expression evaluating to true. Repro steps run in a dev harness mirrored customer config. Reproduced with token missing 'entitlements'. Additional tests: - token with entitlements: ['readonly'] -> correctly allowed - token with entitlements: ['admin'] -> correctly denied - token with absent entitlements -> incorrectly allowed. Root cause hypothesis: backward-compatible change in the policy-eval library (v2.14.0) introduced value coercion for absent claims. Related PR suspected: https://github.com/redwood-inference/authorization/commit/5f7e2b3. Impact surface: Private deployments that rely on omission semantics for exclusion policies. Risk: Moderate-high for private customers using exclusion-based RBAC. Workaround: Advise Atlas Retail to set entitlements claim to empty array for service accounts and short-lived tokens; this required a small IdP mapping change. Temporary policy recommendation provided: add explicit exists(user.entitlements) and deny if not exists. Fix: AuthZ team prepared fix to treat absent claims as empty set in 'not_in' semantics and to avoid coercing absent -> empty string. Patch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/authorization/pull/869. Deployment plan: canary merge to staging on 2026-03-15, rolling release to hosted and a patch bundle for private control plane customers on 2026-03-18. Follow-ups: document 'missing-claim' semantics in policy language reference; add unit tests for absent-claim cases.

The root cause of the March 2026 incident was a **race condition in the `sse-gateway`** [1]. Specifically, a mid-flight upstream TCP RST (caused by an edge-proxy idle RST during a network hiccup) caused an in-flight terminal chunk flush and a scheduled keepalive/heartbeat frame to interleave [1]. This led to the terminal 'end' event being dropped and the gateway retransmitting a heartbeat while the `serving-runtime` was simultaneously finalizing the stream [1]. Additionally, the Nimbus client SDK attempted to resume immediately with `last_seq`, which caused the gateway to interleave a replayed heartbeat with the resumed payload [1].

The server-side fix involved rolling out **inference-runtime PR 2147**, which implemented the following:
*   **Atomic Emission:** Forced the atomic emission of the terminal 'end' event [1, 2].
*   **Stronger Ordering:** Ensured stronger ordering of keepalive/heartbeat frames by placing them behind the terminal flush [1, 2].
*   **Client Backoff:** Applied a short backoff on client resume acceptance to better tolerate in-flight socket tear-downs [1].
